strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-supported empirical analysis of the detection-association conflict in MOTR, quantitatively confirming (Table 1, Fig. 2, Table 9) that removing track queries substantially boosts detection AP, and that this gap can be nearly eliminated (66.3->71.2 AP without track queries vs 70.9 with, i.e. -0.3 drop instead of -6.3) with the proposed method.

A systematic and informative ablation across four distinct prior-injection mechanisms (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) offers a useful comparative study for the community, going beyond a single proposed technique.

The resulting SelfMOTR method is conceptually simple and fully detector-free/end-to-end, in contrast to MOTRv2/MOTRv3 which rely on an external pretrained detector, which is a genuine practical/architectural advantage that reduces pipeline complexity and dependency on domain-matched external detectors.

Reasonably thorough set of ablations (proposal source, confidence threshold, data augmentation/CrowdHuman joint training, decoder depth vs. accuracy trade-off, runtime/FPS profiling) supports the design choices and gives practitioners actionable insight (e.g., a shallow proposal decoder suffices).
The runtime analysis is a nice addition, showing the dual-pass design only incurs ~17% FPS overhead because the heavy encoder is shared and only the lightweight decoder runs twice.
weaknesses: Overall performance is only roughly on par with (not exceeding) existing end-to-end trackers on DanceTrack (69.2 vs. CO-MOT's 69.4 HOTA) and is clearly below several strong end-to-end baselines on MOT17 (57.5 vs. 60.2 MOTRv3, 60.1 CO-MOT), which weakens the claim of a strong new contribution to state-of-the-art tracking; the detector-free design seems to hurt notably on the more detection-sensitive MOT17 benchmark, and this trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

The core technical idea (a detection-only forward pass generating region/anchor proposals that are then refined by a second decoder pass) closely echoes the two-stage mechanism already present in Deformable DETR and is conceptually similar to MOTRv2's anchor-injection strategy, just internally self-generated; the novelty is therefore relatively incremental rather than a fundamentally new architectural idea.

Evaluation is limited to two datasets (DanceTrack and MOT17) with no results on MOT20, BDD100K, or other more crowded/diverse tracking benchmarks, limiting evidence for general applicability of the method.

As acknowledged by the authors, the self-proposal mechanism is only tested on the base MOTR architecture, not integrated into more competitive modern baselines such as CO-MOT or MOTRv3, leaving open whether the approach would provide complementary gains or be redundant with their existing conflict-mitigation strategies.

No reported variance/multiple-seed results, and no code/reproducibility artifacts (e.g., public repository) are mentioned, which is a concern given the many architectural and training details (e.g., proposal threshold, learned anchor count, loss weighting) that could affect reproducibility.

The writing in places (e.g., related work) is informal, and some ablation tables/statements (e.g., why self-proposal underperforms anchor-proposal-from-frozen-detector on some metrics in Table 6) are not fully explained, leaving some inconsistencies not sufficiently discussed.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and recognized problem in end-to-end MOT transformers: the detection-association conflict in MOTR-style architectures.

The empirical observation that MOTR exhibits substantially better detection performance with track queries removed (Table 1, Fig. 2) is a clean and interesting diagnostic finding that motivates the rest of the work.

The systematic ablation across four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) in Table 2 is a reasonably thorough empirical analysis that provides useful insight into which mechanisms help and why.

The proposed self-proposal mechanism is simple, requires no external detector, and is shown to nearly eliminate the detection-association AP gap (Table 9: -6.3 to -0.3), which is a compelling piece of evidence for the core claim.

The efficiency analysis (shared encoder, shallow decoder for proposals, FPS comparison, decoder-depth study) is a useful practical contribution showing the method is not costly despite the dual-pass design.
weaknesses: The core idea is an incremental recombination of existing techniques (anchor-proposal mechanisms akin to MOTRv2, self-distillation/self-training ideas) rather than a fundamentally new concept; the paper's own discussion section struggles to clearly differentiate itself from MOTRv2-style approaches beyond removing the external detector.

Results are only on par with or slightly below existing end-to-end methods (CO-MOT, MOTRv3) on DanceTrack and clearly below several baselines on MOT17 (Table 4: SelfMOTR 57.5 HOTA vs CO-MOT 60.1, MOTRv3 60.2, and even underperforms vanilla MOTR-family DetA), undermining the practical impact claim despite the architectural novelty.

Evaluation is limited to only two datasets (DanceTrack, MOT17) and a single backbone/base architecture (MOTR); the authors acknowledge in Limitations that the method is not tested on stronger architectures like CO-MOT or MOTRv3, which considerably limits generalizability claims.

No standard deviations, multiple seeds, or statistical significance analysis are reported for any of the results, which is concerning given that many reported gains (e.g., some ablation deltas in Tables 2, 6, 8) are small and could be within run-to-run variance for MOT/DanceTrack training.

The qualitative/intuitive explanation of why self-proposals reduce interference (feature-space alignment) is asserted but not rigorously validated, e.g., via feature-level analysis, visualization of query evolution, or controlled studies isolating this specific claim.

The MOT17 results are notably weaker than DanceTrack, and the paper offers only a brief, somewhat hand-wavy explanation (detector-sensitive benchmark) without deeper analysis of why the self-proposal benefit does not transfer as effectively; this weakens the generality of the proposed solution.

The method still requires two decoder passes per frame, and while FPS overhead is modest, the actual GFLOPs/parameter overhead and training cost beyond FPS are not discussed, obscuring the full computational trade-off.

The paper's novelty largely rests on a known observation already reported in cited prior work (CO-MOT/[23]) that MOTR's detection improves without track queries; the contribution is primarily in operationalizing this known observation rather than discovering it, which somewhat limits the originality claim in the introduction.

strengths: The central empirical observation—that MOTR-style models contain a much stronger 'hidden' detector that is suppressed once track queries are activated (Fig. 2, Table 1)—is clearly demonstrated and provides a compelling motivation for the work.

The systematic comparison of four prior-injection strategies (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal) in Section 3.1/Table 2 is a valuable ablation study that helps isolate which mechanism actually matters, going beyond a single proposed trick.

The proposed SelfMOTR method is conceptually simple and practical: it removes the need for an external detector while still injecting a useful detection prior, preserving the fully end-to-end nature of MOTR-style trackers.

Table 9's direct before/after comparison of detection AP with/without track queries for the self-proposal architecture (drop of only -0.3 vs. -6.3 for vanilla MOTR) is convincing quantitative evidence that the detection-association conflict is substantially mitigated.

The ablation suite is thorough: proposal source (Table 6), confidence threshold (Table 8), decoder depth (Fig. 5), data augmentation interactions (Table 7), and runtime/efficiency profiling (Table 10) collectively give good insight into the design choices and their individual contributions.
Results on DanceTrack are competitive with recent end-to-end SOTA methods (CO-MOT, MOTRv3) while avoiding reliance on an external detector, which is a meaningful practical benefit.
weaknesses: MOT17 results (57.5 HOTA) clearly underperform several end-to-end baselines including CO-MOT (60.1) and MOTRv3 (60.2), which somewhat undercuts the claim of being broadly competitive with SOTA; the paper attributes this to the detector-free design but does not further test this hypothesis on other detector-sensitive benchmarks.

The self-proposal mechanism (a lightweight decoder pass generating anchors that are refined by a shared decoder) closely resembles the two-stage proposal generation used in Deformable DETR and other two-stage detectors; the paper does not discuss this connection, which somewhat tempers the novelty claim beyond applying an established idea to the tracking setting.

Ablation results in Table 2 (e.g., Query Pretraining, Detection Pretraining) show quite small differences (e.g., 0.2-0.3 point changes) without any indication of variance across seeds, making it hard to assess whether these differences are statistically meaningful.

The strong DanceTrack gains are partly entangled with additional training ingredients (HSV augmentation, joint CrowdHuman training, denoising) as shown in Table 5/7; while the paper does show self-proposals scale better with this data, it would help to clarify whether the comparison to CO-MOT/MOTRv3 in Table 3 uses matched data/augmentation settings for a fully fair comparison.

The paper is instantiated only on the older MOTR/MOTRv2 architecture rather than more advanced query-based baselines (CO-MOT, MOTRv3), which the authors acknowledge as a limitation; this leaves open whether the proposed self-proposal mechanism would still yield gains (or be redundant) when combined with these already more sophisticated detection-association decoupling strategies.

Efficiency reporting is limited to a single FPS comparison; a more detailed compute/parameter overhead breakdown (e.g., FLOPs of the extra decoder pass across different proposal counts) would strengthen the practical efficiency claims.

strengths: Strong motivating analysis: the paper convincingly demonstrates via Fig. 2 and the four-strategy ablation in Table 1 that MOTR-style joint decoders retain substantial 'hidden' detection capacity that is suppressed by joint detection-association training, providing a clear empirical basis for the proposed method.

The proposed Track Attention Mass diagnostic, adapted from attention-sink analysis in LLMs, is a novel and interpretable lens for understanding query interference in joint decoders, and is applied consistently across three datasets (Fig. 5, Fig. 7) to support the paper's narrative.

SelfMOTR is conceptually simple and practical: it removes the need for an external pretrained detector (unlike MOTRv2/MOTRv3) while avoiding the complex shadow-query management of CO-MOT, achieving this via a lightweight second decoder pass that reuses the same backbone/encoder features.

Extensive ablations are provided, covering successive component addition (Table 6), proposal source comparison (Table 7), proposal confidence threshold (Table 4c), decoder depth for the proposal pass (Fig. 6), and data scaling (Table 4b), giving a reasonably complete picture of design choices.

Competitive/strong empirical results: near state-of-the-art on DanceTrack among end-to-end methods, a new best HOTA on the BFT dataset (71.1), and best-in-class among end-to-end trackers on AnimalTrack, along with honest additional results on MOT17 showing where the approach still falls short.

Runtime overhead is modest and clearly reported (24.8 → 20.7 FPS), and the paper shows this overhead can be reduced further by using a shallow decoder for the proposal pass without much accuracy loss.
weaknesses: The headline DanceTrack result is essentially on par with CO-MOT (69.2 vs 69.4 HOTA) and behind the non-fully-end-to-end MOTRv2 (69.9), so the empirical case for superiority is mixed rather than clearly established; gains are concentrated in specific sub-metrics (AssA, IDF1) rather than an unambiguous overall win.

MOT17 results (Table 5) are notably weaker than several existing end-to-end and non-end-to-end methods, and the paper's own discussion acknowledges this gap is not closed, raising questions about the generality of the proposed self-proposal mechanism beyond DanceTrack-like domains.

The core architectural idea—running a lightweight detection-only decoder pass to generate proposals that are then merged with propagated track queries—is conceptually close to two-stage/RPN-style proposal generation and to existing prior-injection strategies (e.g., MOTRv2's anchor proposals), the main departure being that the 'detector' is now the same model's own weights rather than an external one; the degree of novelty is somewhat incremental.

The Track Attention Mass analysis and its cross-dataset interpretation (Fig. 7, e.g., the claim that BFT's non-rigid deformation causes higher reliance on track history) are largely descriptive/post-hoc and not validated with targeted causal experiments (e.g., intervening on entropy or mass to test the hypothesized mechanism), so the explanatory claims remain speculative.

On AnimalTrack, SelfMOTR underperforms the non-end-to-end QDTrack baseline (45.5 vs 47.0 HOTA), which is understated in the text that instead emphasizes a favorable comparison against TrackFormer; this selective framing slightly overstates the generalization claim.

Reproducibility is a concern: the project page link is left as a placeholder, and no explicit code/data release commitment is stated, despite the method depending on several tuned hyperparameters (proposal confidence threshold, number of learned fallback anchors, loss weight λ_prop).

strengths: The core motivation is clearly articulated and supported by a well-designed preliminary experiment (Fig. 2) showing that MOTR's detection accuracy drops when track queries are active, substantiating the detection-association conflict claim.

The paper performs a thorough, systematic ablation (Fig. 3, Table 1) comparing four different mechanisms for injecting detection priors (pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal), which is informative beyond just presenting the final method.

The proposed Track-Attention Mass / normalized entropy diagnostic is a reasonably novel and interpretable tool for analyzing query interference in joint decoders, and the cross-dataset analysis (Fig. 7) linking attention regime to target dynamics (e.g., BFT vs DanceTrack) is a nice qualitative insight.
Evaluation spans multiple datasets (DanceTrack, BFT, AnimalTrack, MOT17) and includes efficiency/runtime considerations (Table 4a, Fig. 6), which strengthens the empirical breadth.
The method is conceptually simple (no external detector, no extra query-management logic like CO-MOT's shadow queries) which is a genuine practical advantage if the gains hold up.
weaknesses: On MOT17, a central and widely-used MOT benchmark, SelfMOTR underperforms the plain MOTR baseline on HOTA (57.5 vs 57.8) and DetA (57.3 vs 60.3), and trails essentially every other listed end-to-end competitor including CO-MOT and MOTRv3. This directly contradicts the paper's central claim that self-generated priors resolve the detection-association conflict, and the paper's own explanation ("genuinely new modeling ideas" needed) effectively concedes the method does not generalize beyond its favorable benchmarks.

On the headline DanceTrack result, SelfMOTR (69.2 HOTA) is marginally below CO-MOT (69.4 HOTA) and MOTRv2 (69.9, albeit non end-to-end), so the paper's "highly competitive" framing somewhat overstates a result that is not actually state of the art even within the end-to-end category on the most standard benchmark.

Table 1 shows that the externally-sourced "Anchor Proposal" baseline (58.0 HOTA) nearly matches the final internal "Self Proposal" design (58.2 HOTA, Table 7), suggesting the key gain comes from using explicit decoupled 4D anchors generically, not specifically from the proposed self-generation mechanism — this weakens the paper's central architectural contribution and novelty claim.

The BFT and AnimalTrack comparisons omit several of the strongest recent end-to-end competitors used in the DanceTrack table (e.g., CO-MOT, MOTRv2, MOTRv3), making the claimed state-of-the-art status on these datasets less convincing and the comparison set inconsistent across tables.

The attention-based diagnostic analysis (Track Attention Mass, entropy) is interesting but largely qualitative and speculative ("we hypothesize"); no statistical tests, confidence intervals, or causal interventions are provided to confirm that the attention patterns actually cause the performance differences rather than merely correlating with them.

Reproducibility is weak: hyperparameters such as the proposal threshold, loss weights, and the number of learned anchors appear tuned per-dataset without a clear held-out validation protocol, and no code/project page link is actually provided in the submission.

The runtime overhead (20.7 vs 24.8 FPS, a ~17% drop) from running the decoder twice is non-trivial and could matter in real-time applications, yet this trade-off is understated relative to the modest accuracy gains shown in some settings.

The paper's title and abstract emphasize broad applicability of the method, but given the MOT17 regression and marginal DanceTrack gains, the actual contribution appears more narrowly scoped to specific dataset regimes (BFT, AnimalTrack) than the framing suggests.

strengths: The paper is built on a well-motivated empirical observation (Fig. 2) that MOTR retains latent detection capability that is suppressed by joint detection-association decoding, and this observation is thoroughly validated before the method is introduced.

The paper provides an unusually thorough set of controlled ablations (Sec. 3.1, Table 1) comparing four distinct strategies for injecting detection priors (detection pretraining, query pretraining, distillation, anchor proposal), which clarifies design choices and gives the reader insight into why the anchor-based/self-proposal mechanism is chosen.

The proposed Track Attention Mass diagnostic (with cardinality correction and normalized entropy) is a reasonable and interpretable tool for probing query interference in decoder self-attention, and is applied consistently across three datasets (Fig. 5, Fig. 7) to support the paper's narrative.

SelfMOTR is detector-free and fully end-to-end, removing dependence on an external pretrained detector (unlike MOTRv2/MOTRv3) while achieving performance competitive with or exceeding methods that do rely on such detectors, notably state-of-the-art HOTA on BFT (71.1) and best-in-class end-to-end results on AnimalTrack.

The efficiency analysis (Table 4a, Fig. 6) demonstrates that the detection-only pass can be shallow, and that overall runtime overhead relative to a single-pass baseline is modest, supporting practical viability.

The detection-association conflict experiment (AP with/without track queries, Table 4a) directly and convincingly demonstrates that SelfMOTR largely removes the interference that plagues vanilla MOTR (AP drop of only 0.3 vs. 6.3 points).
weaknesses: Results on the standard MOT17 benchmark (Table 5, appendix) are noticeably weaker than existing end-to-end methods (CO-MOT, MOTRv3) and substantially behind non-end-to-end trackers (e.g., SPAM at 67.5 HOTA vs. SelfMOTR's 57.5-58.4), yet this important negative result is relegated to the appendix and not discussed prominently in the main text/conclusion, somewhat undercutting the generality of the claims.

The gain of the final 'Self Proposal' mechanism over the externally-sourced '4D Anchor Proposal' baseline is marginal (58.2 vs 58.0 HOTA in Table 1/Table 7), which weakens the central claim that internally generated priors are meaningfully better than externally sourced ones from an already-trained detector — the main advantage appears to be avoiding an extra model rather than a clear performance improvement.

The Track Attention Mass analysis, while insightful, is largely correlational/descriptive; the paper does not perform a causal intervention (e.g., directly manipulating attention mass and measuring downstream tracking effect) to firmly establish that this attention imbalance is the causal mechanism behind the detection-association conflict, rather than just a symptom.

On DanceTrack, SelfMOTR's headline HOTA (69.2) is essentially on par with, not better than, CO-MOT (69.4), and DetA is lower (80.9 vs 82.1); the paper's framing as 'highly competitive' is accurate but the improvement narrative is somewhat oversold relative to the actual numbers.

Most ablations (thresholds, HSV/CrowdHuman augmentation, proposal source, decoder depth) are conducted only on DanceTrack validation, leaving open whether these design choices (e.g., cprop=0.05, Nlearned=10) generalize to BFT/AnimalTrack or require re-tuning.
No variance/multiple-run statistics are reported for the main results or ablations, making it hard to judge whether small differences (e.g., 0.2-0.3 HOTA/AP) are meaningful or within noise.
The project page link is left blank, and full training/inference code availability is not explicitly confirmed, which is a minor but relevant reproducibility concern.
